Chapter: 3. DEFENSE MECHANISMS OF GINGIVA & HOST RESPONSE
Question: The predominant cell type in gingival crevicular fluid is the:
Explanation:
The predominant cell type in GCF is the PMN. They account for 92% of the total leukocytes while the mononuclear cells account for 8%. Mononuclear cells were identified as 58% B lymphocytes, 24% T lymphocytes, and 18% mononuclear phagocytes.

Among the mononuclear cells, 58% are B-lymphocytes and 24% are T-lymphocytes. The normal T:B lymphocyte ratio in peripheral blood is 3:1 and the value is reversed to about 1:3 in GCF.

In GCF ratio of T:B cells: 1:3.

Question: Gingival crevicular fluid is measured using:
Explanation:
Methods of collecting GCF:
• Placing filter paper into the sulcus (intracrevicular)
• Placing paper at the entrance of sulcus (extra crevicular)
• Placing preweighed twisted threads or micropipettes and crevicular washings.

Methods of measuring the amount of GCF:
• The wetted area of the filter paper is stained with Ninhydrin and is measured planimetrically under microscope.
• Electronic method by using fluid collected on a blotter (Perio paper) and employing electronic transducer called Periotron.

Paper points, micropipette and preweighed twisted threads are used to collect GCF.

Question: Predominant immunoglobulin in GCF/ Crevicular fluid is
Explanation:
• Predominant immunoglobulin in GCF – IgG
• Predominant immunoglobulin in Saliva – IgA
• Although immunoglobulins G (IgG) and M (IgM) are present, the predominant immunoglobulin found in saliva is immunoglobulin A (IgA). Major and minor salivary glands contribute all the secretory IgA (sIgA) and lesser amounts of IgG and IgM.
• It has been shown that IgA antibodies present in parotid saliva can inhibit the attachment of oral Streptococcus species to epithelial cells.

Question: PMNs lying freely in saliva
Explanation: Orogranulocytes are the PMNs that reach the oral cavity by migrating through the lining of the gingival sulcus and their rate of migration into the oral cavity is termed the orogranulocytic migratory rate. Some investigators believe the rate of migration correlates with the severity of gingival inflammation and is therefore a reliable index for assessing gingivitis.

Explanation:

Concentration of tetracycline in gingival fluid is 2-10 times (average 7 times) that of plasma.

Question: Glucose levels in gingival crevicular fluid (GCF) are:
Option A: Equal to glucose level in serum
Option D: More than 10 times the serum levels
Explanation:
Glucose concentration in GCF is 3–4 times greater than in serum. This is not only due to the metabolic activity of adjacent tissues, but also as a function of the local microbial flora.

The protein content of GCF is less than that of serum.

Explanation: Leukotoxin is an exotoxin produced by A. actinomycetemcomitans which has toxic effect on PMN’s. This enables these microorganisms to evade the host defense phagocytosis.

Explanation:
Interleukin 1 (a and b) includes Osteoclast Activating Factor (OAF) which causes bone resorption and Lymphocyte Activating Factor (LAF) which has the ability to stimulate proliferation of T cells.

IL-1 and TNF (Tumor necrosis factor) are key cytokines in the pathogenesis of periodontitis.

Question: Plaque is considered as infection because
Option B: Its presence is evidence of bacterial growth
Option C: It is communicable between experimental animals and probably humans
Explanation:
Robert Koch developed the criteria by which a microorganism can be judged to be the causative agent in human infections. These are called as “Koch’s postulates”.

SIGMOND SOCRANSKY proposed criteria by which periodontal microorganisms may be judged to be potential pathogens. They are:
• Be associated with disease with increase in number of organisms at diseased sites.
• Be eliminated or decreased with treatment.
• Demonstrate host response.
• Demonstrate virulence factors.
• Be capable of causing disease in experimental animals.

The pathogenic potential of bacteria within the plaque varies from individual to individual and from one gingival site to other gingival site.

Question: Gingival fluid is a:
Option C: Can be either of the two (Trasudate & Exudate)
Explanation:
Gingival crevicular fluid (GCF) can be either a transudate or an exudate depending on the condition of the gingiva. In healthy people, GCF is primarily a transudate — a fluid that passes through a membrane or tissue due to hydrostatic or osmotic pressure without inflammation.

During inflammation, however, the gingival fluid flow increases, and its composition starts to resemble that of an inflammatory exudate.

Question: What are the cells that produce PGE2 in the Periodontium?
Explanation: The cells that produce PGE₂ (Prostaglandin E₂) in periodontium are macrophages and fibroblasts. PGE₂ induces the secretion of metallomatrix proteins and osteoclastic bone resorption and contributes to the loss of alveolar bone loss as seen in periodontitis.

Question: The bacterial enzyme detected in gingival crevicular fluid is
Explanation:
The enzymes in GCF can be host derived or produced by the bacteria in the gingival crevice. The following enzymes are detected in GCF:
• Beta-glucuronidase (lysosomal enzyme)
• Lactic acid dehydrogenase (Cytoplasmic enzyme)
• Collagenases (from PMN, fibroblasts or bacterial origin)
• Phospholipases (lysosomal enzyme)

The majority of GCF elements detected thus far are the enzymes.

Option B: Diffuse red lesion of the attached gingiva.
Explanation:
The periodontal lesions seen in HIV-infected patients are:
• Linear gingival erythema / HIV-Gingivitis: The erythematous, easily bleeding gingiva may be limited to marginal gingiva or may be diffuse extending into attached gingiva (AP-16).
• Necrotising ulcerative gingivitis.

Subject: Periodontics
Question: Lateral food impaction occurs mainly due to
Option A: Un even alteration of occlusal surface
Explanation:
Factors causing vertical food impaction are:
• Uneven occlusal wear.
• Opening of the contact point.
• Improperly constructed restorations.

The cusps that tend to forcibly wedge food into interproximal embrasures are known as PLUNGER CUSPS. Disto lingual cusp of upper 2nd molar is commonest plunger cusp.

Lateral pressure from the lips, cheeks and tongue may force food interproximally. This is called as lateral food impaction. This is more likely to occur when the gingival embrasure is enlarged by tissue destruction in periodontal disease.
